A regular wave and a one-off spike produce similar CVs and demand opposite responses — the first is fixed by planning around the season, the second by syncing purchasing with the promo calendar, and neither is fixed by safety stock.

A practical note on the snack: a self-inflicted promo spike sitting in the sales history is dangerous beyond XYZ too. If it stays in the data as ordinary demand, any forecasting model will bake in its repeat next June — and the warehouse will end up bracing for a peak nobody actually planned.

tasks.title: What to do with each cell
tasks.brief: The ABC-XYZ matrix is built, nine cells are filled in. The logistics director asks for one rule per cell: where to hold stock, where not to, and what to do with the borderline items.
tasks.goal: Tie each cell of the matrix to a specific action.
tasks.scenario:
ABC-XYZ matrix, four
characteristic items:

  AX  1.5L water
    large revenue,
    steady demand
  AZ  150g snack
    large revenue,
    demand swings
  CX  kids' yogurt
    small revenue,
    steady demand
  CZ  0.2L juice
    small revenue,
    demand swings

Warehouse space is limited,
holding safety stock on
everything is impossible.
tasks.predictQuestion: What allocation of effort is correct?

options.label: AX: precise stock calculation and auto-ordering, since a mistake here is the costliest; AZ: the main target for manual attention and safety stock; CX: a simple replenishment rule with no human involved; CZ: a candidate for order-to-demand or delisting
options.why: Attention is allocated by the product of a mistake's cost and its likelihood. AX is expensive but predictable, so it gets automated. AZ is expensive and unpredictable — it's the one cell where manual work actually pays off.

options.label: All attention on group A as a whole, group C ordered on a leftover basis
options.why: Half right: A really does matter more by money. But within A, AX and AZ need opposite treatment — the first can be trusted to auto-order, the second can't, and that's exactly the distinction XYZ provides.

options.label: Safety stock across every X item: demand is steady there, so shortages are unacceptable
options.why: The opposite: steady demand is exactly what lets you get by with a minimal buffer, because it forecasts well. Safety stock is the price of uncertainty, and it belongs where uncertainty actually is.

options.label: Delist the group C items: they contribute little revenue and take up warehouse space
options.why: A mechanical delist based on one cell is a common and expensive mistake. An item can be small in revenue and still necessary: it's what draws people into the store, it fills out a lineup a chain requires, or it holds the brand's shelf presence.

hints: For each cell, ask two things: how much does a mistake cost, and how likely is it?
Safety stock is needed where demand is unpredictable, not where it's large.
tasks.explain:
The point of the matrix isn't classification, it's that each cell calls for its own action. ABC answers how much a mistake costs; XYZ answers how likely it is. Multiply them and you get an allocation of attention: where a person is needed, where a rule suffices, and where it's worth dropping the item entirely.

AX — money with predictable demand: an ideal candidate for automatic ordering. The math is worked out once, then the system runs itself, and the freed-up attention goes where it's actually needed. AZ is the cell the whole matrix exists for: the mistake is expensive and likely, no formula will save you, it needs a person, a bigger buffer, and syncing with the promo calendar. CX — small stuff with steady demand: a simple replenishment rule, minimal involvement. CZ — small stuff that also swings: order to demand, minimal stock, and if problems are persistent, a question about delisting.

The main caveat is about delisting group C items. The matrix is built on one metric and knows nothing about an item's role in the assortment. A kids' yogurt might contribute a small percent of revenue and still be the reason a family picks your brand over the one next to it; a flavor lineup might be a condition of a chain contract. The delisting decision gets made after a conversation with the category manager, not off a matrix cell.

The second caveat is about recomputing. The matrix is a snapshot for a period, and an item moves between cells: a new product starts in C, a seasonal item shifts XYZ groups depending on the calculation window, and a declining brand slides into C while staying important. It's worth recomputing quarterly, and watching the transitions matters as much as the current position: a move from AX to BZ is a signal by itself, before it even shows up in revenue.

tasks.title: Water and juice rise together
tasks.brief: A marketer noticed that monthly sales of «Aqualis» water and «Fruvia» juice through 2025 move almost in step, and proposes shelving them as a pair: "the juice pulls the water along." Before the budget defense, the head of the team asks for the link to be checked.
tasks.goal: Work out what a correlation of 0.84 proves, and why the second number refutes it.
tasks.scenario:
Sales in units, 2025:

  month      «Aqualis»   «Fruvia»
  January         6 510      5 756
  February        5 663      4 357
  April          17 482     10 567
  June           21 181      9 266
  July           15 792      8 702
  November        6 499      4 291
  December        8 162      5 396

Correlation of the two series:

  monthly sales 2025           0.84
  year-over-year changes       0.10

  (in the second line each month
  is compared with the same month
  a year earlier, 18 pairs)
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this pair of numbers say about the link between the two brands?

options.label: The joint movement is explained by a common cause: the season. As soon as each month is compared with the same month a year earlier, the link all but disappears
options.why: The season lifts both drinks in summer and pushes both down in winter. The 0.84 correlation describes that shared wave, not a link between the brands: year over year the wave is subtracted from both series, and 0.10 is all that's left of the link.

options.label: 0.84 is a strong link, the juice really does pull the water along; the second number just says year-over-year data is noisier
options.why: Noise would lower the correlation moderately. A fall from 0.84 to 0.10 isn't noise — it means the first correlation rested entirely on a factor that the second calculation removes.

options.label: There is a link, but it runs the other way: the water pulls the juice, because it sells in larger volumes
options.why: Correlation is symmetric and contains no direction at all: swap the columns and you get the same number. You can't extract from it what precedes what, let alone what causes what.

options.label: Not enough data: twelve months is too short a series to draw conclusions from
options.why: Series length is a real limitation, but it's beside the point here. The problem isn't that 0.84 was computed unreliably — it's that even a perfectly precise coefficient doesn't answer the question "what caused what."

hints: Look at what April, June and July have in common — and what November and February lack.
Compare the two calculations against each other: what exactly changed in the second one, and why did that kill the link?
tasks.explain:
Correlation answers exactly one question: do two series move in step. It doesn't answer "what is the cause," "what is the effect," or "is there any link between them at all" — and that isn't nitpicking over wording, it's the difference between a sound decision and a harmful one.

What's at work here is the most common of the three traps — a shared third factor. In summer, sales of both water and juice go up because it's hot; in winter both fall. Neither brand influences the other, but the series walk hand in hand, and the coefficient honestly reports 0.84. Shelving them as a pair would buy the company not a sales increase but a coincidence that would have happened anyway.

The check that exposes a link like this is simple: remove the common factor and see what's left. Comparing each month with the same month a year earlier subtracts the season from both series at once — and the correlation drops to 0.10, which is zero up to randomness. If the brands really were linked — if shoppers genuinely bought them together — the link would survive that procedure: a good month for one would still be a good month for the other after the season came out.

The other two traps are worth keeping in mind as the same short list. Reverse causation: "outlets with larger stock have higher sales" — more likely stock is held where sales are already high. And selection: comparing groups that objects didn't enter at random — that's the next task.

What to do in practice. When you see a correlation, ask three questions in a row: what third factor could have lifted both series, could the arrow point the other way, and how did the objects end up in the groups being compared. If none of them has a clear answer, the correlation remains an observation, not grounds for a decision. Stating it honestly isn't hard either: "sales move together" is true, "the juice pulls the water" is already a claim about cause, and that has to be proven separately.

tasks.title: Salesperson of the year
tasks.brief: The head of sales pays bonuses on the absolute revenue of the outlets a rep serves. For 2025, rep Sakura Tanaka came first in the FMCG Kanto team and second in the company. The manager wants to unpack what she does and roll it out to everyone else.
tasks.goal: Determine what this ranking actually measures.
tasks.scenario:
Reps ranked by revenue of the
outlets they serve, 2025:

  1  Haruka Yamada          8 outlets
     FMCG Kansai       5 042 930 ¥
  2  Sakura Tanaka         2 outlets
     FMCG Kanto      4 616 915 ¥
  3  Miyu Hayashi    7 outlets
     FMCG Kanto      4 335 843 ¥

Second place's portfolio:

  Sokuhai (Kawaguchi
  warehouse), e-com    4 591 844 ¥
  Yasuragi Store #1057,
  Yokohama                  25 071 ¥

Average 2025 revenue per outlet
by channel:

  e-com                3 222 912 ¥
  pharmacy               345 636 ¥
  chain                  277 651 ¥
  traditional retail      21 706 ¥
tasks.predictQuestion: What does this ranking measure?

options.label: The make-up of the territory, not the person's work: 99.5% of the result came from a single e-com warehouse, where the average outlet brings in 148 times more than in traditional retail
options.why: The reps didn't land in this ranking at random: one had a nationwide marketplace's warehouse in the portfolio, another had eight ordinary stores. The gap between channels is larger than any gap in quality of work, so the ranking ranks territories.

options.label: The work: this person hit record revenue off just two outlets, which is efficiency in its purest form
options.why: Revenue per outlet here is set by the channel, not by anything the person did. The same warehouse in someone else's portfolio would produce roughly the same result — and that's a checkable claim, not a guess: the other seven e-com outlets average 3.2M ¥ each.

options.label: The ranking is right, it just needs normalizing by the number of outlets
options.why: Dividing by outlet count doesn't fix it, it makes it worse: the same portfolio gives 2.3M ¥ per outlet against 630 thousand for first place. The problem isn't the number of outlets, it's that the channels aren't comparable — the comparison has to be made within a channel.

options.label: There's an error in the data: one outlet can't produce 4.6M ¥ when the whole company's revenue is 51.5M ¥
options.why: It can, and it isn't an error. An e-com warehouse ships to a whole region, so in a report it looks like a single "outlet" with the turnover of a small chain. It should be set against another warehouse, not against a store.

hints: Look not at the total but at what it's made of: how much did each outlet in the portfolio contribute?
Ask what would have happened if that warehouse had gone to a different rep.
tasks.explain:
This is the selection trap: objects didn't land in the groups being compared at random, and the difference between the groups arose before the thing you're measuring. Here territories were handed out before the year began, and along with a territory a person got a channel — and channel fixes the order of magnitude of revenue harder than anything else does: 3.2M ¥ per e-com outlet against 21.7 thousand in traditional retail, a gap of a hundred and forty-eight times.

What makes it treacherous is that the ranking isn't technically broken. The numbers are right, the formula is transparent, there's nothing to argue with. What's wrong is the step from number to conclusion: "higher in the ranking" turns into "works better," though an unobserved assumption sits between them — that the territories are comparable. Say it out loud and the whole construction collapses.

The consequences of a KPI like this are worse than an unfair bonus. First, unpacking the leader's practice will come up empty: there's nothing to copy, the advantage isn't in technique. Second, the metric starts steering behavior — reps will compete for territory rather than for sales, and that's rational behavior under this rule. Third, genuinely strong people in weak channels will never come into view.

What gets fixed is the comparison, not the formula. Compare like with like: within a channel, and better still against itself over time (growth of the portfolio's outlets versus last year), because a person's territory doesn't change over the year while the result does. Good practice is to look at an indicator the person actually influences: plan fulfillment on their own territory, brand presence, the number of outlets that started stocking a new product.

The general reflex: when you see a ranking of people, units or regions, ask what set them apart before the measurement began. If it set them apart strongly, the ranking measures that difference rather than merit, and no amount of normalizing cures it.

tasks.title: What proves the promo caused the lift
tasks.brief: The «Krosti: 2+1» promo ran in chains for five weeks, 11 August to 8 September 2025. The brand's chain sales tripled. Trade marketing is taking that number to next year's budget defense; the CFO asks for proof that the promo is what produced the lift.
tasks.goal: Choose the comparison that proves the promo's effect.
tasks.scenario:
Units over the five promo weeks
against the five weeks before:

                     before   promo
  «Krosti»
    chains (promo ran) 1 515   4 869
    trad. retail         130     127
    e-com              4 262   4 486
  Other FMCG brands
    chains            13 809  11 448
tasks.predictQuestion: What in this table proves the promo produced the lift in chains?

options.label: The three lower rows: the same brand in channels with no promo, and other brands in the same channel. Not one of those series grew, so there was no general movement that could account for +221%
options.why: A control group is whatever lived through the same weeks but got no treatment. Here there are two of them: the brand without a promo in other channels, and the channel with the promo but other brands. Both held flat or fell, so tripling can't be pinned on the season, the weather or a general lift in chains.

options.label: The first row: a threefold rise in the channel where the promo ran; a before-and-after comparison is the proof
options.why: A before-and-after comparison doesn't separate the promo's effect from everything else that happened in those weeks: the end of summer, the back-to-school season, a competitor's moves. That's precisely why the first row needed three more.

options.label: The 17% drop in other brands is cannibalization, and it means there was no real growth: shoppers just moved their money around
options.why: Cannibalization is the right next question, but it has to be checked separately and in units of comparable categories: a snack and water compete weakly. And crucially, it doesn't cancel the growth — «Krosti» gained 3 354 units, while other brands lost less than that within its category.

options.label: Nothing: on observational data causation can't be proven in principle, you need a proper experiment
options.why: An experiment really is stronger, but "either an experiment or no conclusions" means, in practice, no conclusions at all. A control group is a workable approximation, and in trade marketing it's the standard, not a compromise.

hints: Ask what should have gone up if the cause were the season or a general market lift rather than the promo.
The three lower rows share one property — which one?
tasks.explain:
Proof of an effect rests not on what happened, but on a comparison with what would have happened without the intervention. That "without" can't be observed directly, so it's replaced with a control group — objects that lived through the same period but got no treatment.

Here the control is double, and that's a strong construction. Along one axis the brand is fixed and the channel varies: «Krosti» in traditional retail and e-com, where there was no promo, stayed put. Along the other the channel is fixed and the brand varies: other FMCG in the same chains over the same weeks fell 17%. If the season or a general lift in chains were producing the growth, it would have shown up in at least one of those rows. It shows up in none — so the explanation is local: the promo.

This line of reasoning has a name — difference-in-differences: you take the change in the treated group and subtract the change in the control. Here the control group actually fell, so an honest estimate of the effect is slightly larger than the observed +221%, not smaller.

Where the construction can break. The control has to be comparable: if the promo ran in chains and traditional retail was taken as the control, the difference in the channels' own dynamics could manufacture an effect by itself. That's covered here by the second control — the same chains. Second: the control must not be affected by the treatment indirectly. If shoppers were shifting money from the snack to water, the control would be "contaminated," and the effect would come out overstated.

The practical takeaway: for any "we did X and the indicator went up," ask for an answer to "and who didn't get X?" With no answer, the conclusion stays a hypothesis — sometimes a plausible one, but never proven. The control group has to be planned before the promo launches, not after: holding a dozen comparable outlets back from the promo costs one week's revenue and buys you the ability to measure the return on every promo that follows.

tasks.title: The first paragraph of the email
tasks.brief: The «Nettora» decline analysis is done: revenue fell 49% because the brand went off the shelf in 46 outlets out of 79, and where it stayed it sells 22% more than before. The email goes to the commercial director, who will read the first two lines on his phone between meetings.
tasks.goal: Choose the first paragraph that makes a decision possible.
tasks.scenario:
Four versions of the opening paragraph:

A  Sending over the analysis of the
   «Nettora» decline for Q2. Attached
   is the extract by outlet, channel
   and region, plus the calculation
   methodology. Happy to discuss.

B  «Nettora» revenue in Q2 2026 was
   1 079 055 ¥ against 2 121 702 ¥
   in Q2 2024. Outlets: 33 against 79.
   Revenue per outlet: 32 699 ¥
   against 26 857 ¥.

C  «Nettora» lost half its revenue
   purely by going off the shelf:
   we are no longer stocked in 46 of
   79 outlets, and where we remain we
   sell 22% more. I suggest starting
   with the five largest lost outlets —
   they bring weighted distribution
   back to 80%, whereas the other
   forty-three together add as much.
   I need your decision on the budget
   for the negotiations.

D  The «Nettora» situation is alarming.
   I believe we urgently need to rethink
   our approach to the brand as a whole —
   from packaging to pricing — or we
   risk losing the category.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which paragraph is written correctly?

options.label: C: the conclusion comes first, the numbers back up that specific conclusion, then a recommendation and an explicit request for a decision
options.why: The reader gets an answer to his question in the first sentence and can decide without opening the attachment. The numbers are selected to support the conclusion rather than dumped wholesale, and the paragraph ends with what's needed from the reader.

options.label: B (facts only, no interpretation): let the manager draw his own conclusion, that's his responsibility
options.why: Drawing the conclusion from these numbers is your job, not his: that's what you did the decomposition for. Handing over four pairs of numbers without a conclusion returns the task to someone who has neither the time nor the context of the calculation. And you lose the chance to explain why price is irrelevant here.

options.label: A: a polite cover note, with the substance in the attachment, where it belongs
options.why: The only thing the reader learns from this paragraph is that the work is done. Attachments get opened only if the first lines force it; a paragraph that doesn't force it turns all the work into a file nobody opens.

options.label: D: the conclusion comes first, and it's decisive enough to get the manager moving
options.why: There is a conclusion, but it doesn't follow from the analysis: the data are about losing the shelf, while the recommendation is about packaging and price. A confident tone is no substitute for a link to the facts, and "rethink the approach as a whole" isn't a decision anyone can take.

hints: Read only the first two lines of each version — that's exactly what the recipient will see. After which one can he decide anything?
Check each version for three things: a conclusion, a number supporting it, and what's required from the reader.
tasks.explain:
There's one rule, and it's an uncomfortable one: the conclusion goes first, ahead of the explanation and ahead of the numbers. Uncomfortable because it runs against the order of the work — you went from data to conclusion and naturally want to lay it out in that order. The reader goes the other way: first "what does this mean for me," and only if the answer matters, "how do we know."

A paragraph structure that works: conclusion, support, recommendation, request. The conclusion is one sentence someone can use to retell you to a third person. The support is the minimum set of numbers that prove that specific conclusion, not every number you have. The recommendation is what you advise doing. The request is what you need from the reader: a decision, a budget, a sign-off, nothing. Without the last item the email stays "for information," and later you wonder why "nothing happened."

Version B is the most widespread analyst's mistake, and it looks virtuous: "I'm not imposing, I'm giving facts." In reality it's shifting the work back. You did the decomposition, you saw that price moved 3% and explains nothing — say so. Selecting numbers to fit the conclusion isn't distortion, it's the substance of the job: showing everything you computed means failing the main task, which is separating what matters from what doesn't.

Version D is the opposite mistake and a more dangerous one. There's a conclusion, it sounds confident, but it's connected to the data only by mood. The check is simple: every claim in the first paragraph must have a number or a fact behind it. "We lost 46 outlets out of 79" — it does. "We need to change the packaging" — follows from nothing you computed.

And a last word on length. The first paragraph exists for the person who won't read further. Everything else — methodology, caveats, breakdowns — lives below and in the attachment, and there it can be as detailed as you like. That isn't cutting the content down, it's ordering it: first what you're being read for, then what you'll use to prove it if asked.

tasks.title: One conclusion, three audiences
tasks.brief: The same «Nettora» analysis has to be told to three people: the CEO at a fifteen-minute committee, the head of the field team, and a fellow analyst who will maintain the report.
tasks.goal: Understand what changes in the delivery from audience to audience, and what never changes.
tasks.scenario:
One and the same fact: the brand lost
46 outlets out of 79, revenue in the
ones that remain grew 22%, and brand
revenue is down 49%.

Three recipients:

  CEO
    decides where the company's
    money goes
  head of the field team
    decides who negotiates
    with whom
  fellow analyst
    will maintain this report
    after you
tasks.predictQuestion: What should change from audience to audience?

options.label: Depth and emphasis: matched to the decision that person makes; the facts and numbers themselves never change
options.why: The CEO needs the scale of the problem and what it's worth; the field lead needs the list of outlets and the order to work them; the analyst needs methodology, filters and the limits of the data. It's one and the same conclusion, cut three ways for three different decisions, not three versions of the truth.

options.label: Only the length changes: shorter for the CEO, longer for the analyst, in between for the field lead
options.why: Length is a consequence, not a decision. The short version for the CEO differs from the short version for the field team not in size but in which fact made it in: what the issue is worth versus which outlets to visit.

options.label: The field team needs it simpler and without numbers: people in the field don't work with analytics every day
options.why: That swaps "for a different decision" for "for less clever people." The field lead needs the most concrete numbers of all — which outlets, in what order, whom to talk to; simplifying them makes the analysis useless exactly where someone will act on it.

options.label: Nothing: all three get the same document, otherwise you end up with three versions of the truth
options.why: A single version of the truth is about numbers and definitions, not about format. One document for everyone means it was written for nobody's decision, and each of them has to hunt for their part in it — and usually doesn't find it.

hints: Ask of each one: what decision will he make tomorrow morning, and which number does he need for it?
One of the options confuses "a different decision" with "simpler, for people who don't get it."
tasks.explain:
Delivery is determined not by the recipient's job title but by the decision they make. That's the only criterion that works: it tells you what to include, in what order, and where to stop.

The CEO needs the scale and the price: half the brand's revenue, a single cause, is it worth investing in a comeback or is closing the line more sensible. He doesn't need the list of outlets — he isn't going to visit them. The head of the field team needs exactly the reverse: which outlets, in what order, which chain is the key one, what to say to the buyer. For him the scale of the problem is one line of context. The fellow analyst needs a third thing: how it was computed, which filters, what counted as an outlet, where the data are unreliable — because his decision is "can this report be trusted, and how do I fix it."

What can't change for any audience are the facts, the numbers, and the caveats that bear on the conclusion. If the analysis has a weak spot — say, some outlets may simply have changed owner rather than dropped the brand — it travels into all three versions, because it changes the conclusion for all three. A caveat you dropped "so as not to overcomplicate things for the CEO" isn't simplification, it's distortion.

A separate word on the temptation to simplify for the field team. It looks like consideration and works like disrespect, and it damages the work: these are precisely the people who need the most concrete data, because they're the ones who will act. The difference between versions isn't in complexity, it's in which slice you put up front.

A practical technique: before writing, finish this sentence on the recipient's behalf — "having read this, I will…". If the sentence doesn't end in an action, the document isn't ready — either you haven't found which decision it serves, or this person doesn't need it at all.

tasks.title: A conclusion you're not sure of
tasks.brief: The analysis is due today. The main conclusion is confirmed, but one part of it rests on data you doubt: some of the lost outlets may not have dropped the brand at all — they may have closed or changed owner, and the reference table doesn't distinguish the two. Checking will take a week.
tasks.goal: Choose the wording that neither lies nor blocks a decision.
tasks.scenario:
Four ways to report this:

A  Say nothing. The conclusion about
   lost distribution is right in the
   main, and a caveat will only confuse
   the reader and weaken the email.

B  "The brand may have lost distribution,
   but the data require further checking,
   so no final conclusions can be drawn
   at this point."

C  "The brand went off the shelf in 46
   outlets out of 79 — that's confirmed
   by sales. Of those 46, some may have
   closed or changed owner: the reference
   table doesn't distinguish the two,
   I'll check against the visit log by
   the 12th. This doesn't affect the
   conclusion — even in the worst case
   losing the shelf remains the main
   cause; it does affect the list of
   priority outlets."

D  Send the analysis in a week, once
   everything is checked: a report with
   caveats is worse than a report
   delivered later.
tasks.predictQuestion: Which version is right?

options.label: C: separate what's confirmed, what's in question and what exactly it affects, with a date for the check
options.why: Three levels of confidence are named explicitly, and crucially it says what the uncertainty affects and what it doesn't. The budget decision can be made today; the decision on the list of outlets after the 12th.

options.label: B: honestly admit the uncertainty and give no conclusion until it's checked
options.why: Formally honest, practically useless: a "may have" with no indication of what specifically is in question and how much it changes the picture reads as "the analyst isn't sure of anything." The reader will either decide blind or not decide at all.

options.label: A (say nothing): the conclusion is right in the main, and a caveat would only weaken the email
options.why: The caveat will surface — at a meeting, from a colleague, or a month later. What suffers then isn't that one number but trust in everything you bring, including the flawless parts. And staying quiet denies the reader the chance to factor the risk into their decision.

options.label: D: send it in a week, once the data are fully checked
options.why: Sometimes that's right, but not here: the confirmed part is enough for the main decision, and a week of standing still costs you negotiations that never started. Completeness bought at the price of being late is also a mistake, just a less visible one.

hints: Ask not "how sure am I" but "what exactly changes in the decision if this part turns out to be wrong."
One of the options is honest in form but gives the reader nothing to work with.
tasks.explain:
Uncertainty is no reason to stay silent and no reason to blur the conclusion. It has to be localized: say which part specifically is in question, how far it could shift the picture, and by when you'll find out.

The construction that works is three levels stated explicitly. What's confirmed: sales stopped in 46 outlets, that's a fact from the data. What's in question: the reason they stopped, because the reference table doesn't distinguish dropping the brand from the outlet closing. What you're doing: a check against the visit log by a specific date. And, as a separate sentence, what it's worth: the uncertainty doesn't affect the main conclusion, it does affect the list of priority outlets. That last part is what turns a caveat from noise into useful information.

Version B is the conscientious analyst's most frequent mistake. It sounds cautious and scientific, but gives the reader nothing: it's unclear what is in question, how serious it is, or when it will be resolved. In practice wording like that most often means the decision gets made without you — on intuition, or on someone else's number that came with no caveats because nobody checked it.

On staying silent, it's worth remembering the mechanics of losing trust. One undeclared weakness coming to light devalues not one number but the whole report: the recipient can't tell the places where you kept quiet from the places where everything is clean, and sensibly hedges on all of it. A declared weakness works the other way — it shows you're in control of the limits of your own knowledge.

And on deadlines. Decisions are made on the calendar, not when the data are ready. The right strategy is almost always to deliver what's confirmed exactly on time, honestly marking the edges, and finish the rest in a separate short message. "I promised by the 12th — here's the result of the check, the conclusion hasn't changed" is worth more than a week of silence.

tasks.title: Four questions, four forms
tasks.brief: Four slides are going into the «Nettora» deck. The designer suggests making all the charts identical — "for a consistent look." You need to decide which form answers each question.
tasks.goal: Match each question to the chart form that answers it.
tasks.scenario:
Four questions in the deck:

  1  How did the brand's revenue move
     week by week over two years?
  2  Which five regions lost the most?
  3  Is an outlet's size related to
     whether it dropped the brand?
  4  What makes up the −49%: how much
     came from losing outlets, how much
     from the change in revenue
     per outlet?
tasks.predictQuestion: Which set of forms is right?

options.label: 1: a line over time; 2: horizontal bars sorted by size; 3: a scatter plot; 4: a waterfall
options.why: Each form encodes exactly what's being asked: a line for continuous change over time, bars for comparing magnitudes across categories, points for the relationship between two numeric quantities, a waterfall for how the parts contribute to a total change.

options.label: 1: bars by week; 2: a pie by region; 3: a line; 4: a table
options.why: Bars over a hundred weeks turn into a picket fence where the trend can't be read. A pie answers a question about shares of a whole, not "who lost the most." A line connects points that have no order between them. A table doesn't show contribution — the reader has to work it out by eye.

options.label: All four as bars: it's the most understandable form, people read it with no explanation
options.why: A form being understandable is no substitute for it fitting the question. Bars really are easy to read, but on a time series of a hundred weeks they hide the very thing the chart is built for — the shape of the change.

options.label: 1: a line; 2: vertical bars; 3: a scatter plot; 4: a pie
options.why: Three of the four are right; the error is in the last one. A pie shows shares of a whole, while the question is about contribution to a change — there are positive and negative parts, and they can't fit into a circle in principle.

hints: For each question, name the type of comparison: over time, across categories, between two numbers, or contribution to a total.
Horizontal bars beat vertical ones when the category names are long — you don't have to tilt them.
tasks.explain:
A chart isn't an illustration for the text, it's a way to answer a question faster than a table can. Hence the single rule for choosing one: state the question in a sentence first, then pick the form that encodes the answer.

Four basic types of comparison cover nearly everything an analyst needs. Change over time — a line: the eye reads slope as speed and breaks as events. Comparison across categories — bars sorted by size, and horizontal ones if the names are long. The relationship between two numeric quantities — a scatter plot, the only form where you see the relationship, its absence, and the outliers alike. Contribution of parts to a change in a total — a waterfall, invented for decomposition specifically.

The pie chart deserves its own word, because it's the default in every editor. Its legitimate territory is narrow: shares of a single whole, when the parts are few, differ markedly, and genuinely sum to a hundred percent. Everything else it does badly — people compare angles worse than lengths, and negative values don't fit into it at all. For the fourth question that disqualifies it immediately: losing outlets pulls down, revenue growth per outlet pushes up.

On sorting and orientation: bars sorted by size answer "who is biggest" instantly, while the same bars in alphabetical order force the reader to sort by eye. That's the cheapest edit in any deck and one of the most noticeable.

And on "a consistent look." What should be consistent is the styling — palette, fonts, axis labels, legend order. The form of the chart obeys the question, not the layout; identical charts for different questions aren't style, they're a refusal to answer.

tasks.title: The axis a conclusion starts from
tasks.brief: The «Vitanor» brand grew 3.2% over the rolling year. Marketing brings a slide where that growth is drawn as bars with the axis starting not at zero but at the series minimum: in the picture the last bar is three times the height of the first.
tasks.goal: Decide where a truncated axis is acceptable and where it turns a chart into a lie.
tasks.scenario:
The same series, two charts:

  bars, axis from zero
    the last bar is higher than
    the first by an amount barely
    visible to the eye (+3.2%)

  bars, axis from the minimum
    the last bar is three times the
    first — it looks like a surge

The number under the chart is the
same in both cases: +3.2%.
tasks.predictQuestion: What's the right answer?

options.label: For bars the axis must start at zero: bar length encodes magnitude, and truncating lies about the ratio. On a line chart truncation is acceptable, but it has to be plainly visible
options.why: A bar is compared by length, so where it starts isn't a styling setting but part of the encoding: truncate the axis and you physically change the ratio the eye reads. A line encodes change through slope and needs no zero base — but a broken scale still gets labeled.

options.label: You must never truncate an axis on any chart: it's a recognized manipulation technique
options.why: The rule is correct for bars and harmful as a universal law: drawing temperature, an exchange rate or market share from zero is pointless — real fluctuations flatten into a straight line and the chart stops showing anything at all.

options.label: Any chart can be truncated as long as an honest number is printed underneath: the number is the source of the conclusion, the picture is just presentation
options.why: The reader believes the picture, not the caption: the shape is the conclusion they carry away. A "+3.2%" under bars that differ threefold doesn't save it — it reads as a technical detail attached to an "obvious" surge.

options.label: For internal reports the scale can be chosen freely; truncation is only unacceptable in external materials
options.why: Internal decisions cost money just as external promises do. Splitting the rule into "among ourselves it's fine" is a short road to the company planning next year's budget off a picture rather than a number.

hints: Ask what exactly the chart uses to encode magnitude: bar length or line slope.
Check the extreme case: what would a chart of the dollar exchange rate look like drawn from zero?
tasks.explain:
The argument about a truncated axis is usually conducted in slogans, but it's settled by one technical question: what does the chart use to encode magnitude?

A bar encodes magnitude with length. The eye compares lengths and concludes something about the ratio: "three times as tall" reads as "three times as much." Truncating the axis doesn't change the caption, but it changes the message itself — the ratio of lengths stops matching the ratio of numbers. That isn't a matter of taste, it's a corruption of the encoding, which is why bars start at zero without exception.

A line encodes magnitude with position and change with slope. It promises nothing about ratios of length, so it doesn't need a zero base and is often hurt by one: an exchange rate, a temperature or a market share drawn from zero flattens out, and the meaningful fluctuations vanish. Here truncation is legitimate, but the break in the scale is marked explicitly and the axis is labeled densely enough for the reader to see the real range.

There's an opposite mistake too, discussed less often. Stretching the axis down to zero where the fluctuations are the point hides the real movement and nudges the reader toward "nothing is happening." Both mistakes are of one kind: the scale was chosen to fit a desired impression rather than the question.

On "+3.2% printed next to the picture." A caption doesn't cure the form, because the two are read at different speeds: the picture instantly and whole, the number only if you linger. A week later what stays in memory is the impression of a surge, not the figure. Check yourself with this question: cover every label — what would a person conclude from the geometry alone? If that conclusion diverges from the number, the chart is wrong, whatever is written underneath.

And something practical: in this particular case 3.2% growth over a year genuinely does look unremarkable on a chart from zero. That isn't a problem with the chart, it's information — the change really is small. If it matters, show it in a different form: a year-over-year chart in percent, say, where 3.2% honestly fills the whole scale.

tasks.title: Twenty-nine slices of pie
tasks.brief: For the slide on portfolio concentration, a pie chart is proposed: 29 SKUs in the FMCG division, each with its share of revenue. The slide's question is "how dependent is the company on a few products."
tasks.goal: Choose the form that answers the slide's question.
tasks.scenario:
What's known about the FMCG portfolio:

  SKUs in total                 29
  the top 20% of SKUs give   36.3%
    of revenue
  to reach 80% of revenue you
    need            20 SKUs of 29

The slide's question: how dependent is
the company on a few products?
tasks.predictQuestion: Which form answers this question?

options.label: A Pareto chart: bars in descending order of share plus a cumulative-percentage line, which reads off directly how many SKUs you need to reach any threshold
options.why: The slide's question is about accumulation, not about individual shares. The cumulative curve answers it geometrically: you can see both that the top is modest and that reaching 80% means going all the way to the twentieth product.

options.label: A pie chart with 29 sectors: the most direct way to show shares of a whole
options.why: Twenty-nine sectors means most of them are thinner than their label. People can't compare angles that size, and a circle doesn't answer a question about accumulation at all: summing sectors by eye is impossible.

options.label: The top 8 products as bars, the rest as a single "other" row
options.why: A respectable form and the best one for many slides, but not for this question: rolling the rest into one "other" row hides exactly what's being asked about — the length of the tail. It would answer a different question, "who are our biggest products."

options.label: A table of all 29 SKUs with shares and a cumulative percentage
options.why: The data are all there, but the reader has to extract the conclusion himself by scanning two dozen rows. A table is good as an appendix to the slide or as a working tool, not as an answer to a question about the degree of concentration.

hints: Reread the slide's question: is it about individual shares, or about how many products it takes to reach a threshold?
Test each form against an action: can you answer "it takes N products to reach 80%" from it without doing arithmetic in your head?
tasks.explain:
The form is chosen to fit the question, and in this task the question is stated with unusual precision: not "what are the products' shares" but "how dependent are we on a few." That's a question about accumulation, and what answers it is a cumulative curve, not a set of shares.

A Pareto chart combines two encodings: descending bars show each product's contribution, the cumulative-percentage line shows how much has been gathered by each rank. The reader runs their eye from the threshold they care about to the curve and gets the answer without computing. On these data they'll see two things at once: the top is small (the top 20% of products give only 36.3%) and the tail is long (reaching 80% of revenue takes twenty products out of twenty-nine). The conclusion — concentration is moderate — matters more for an assortment decision than any individual share.

On a pie with two dozen sectors: the problem isn't aesthetics, it's that it doesn't answer. Even if a person could compare thin angles, they can't sum them by eye — and the question demands precisely a sum. The general rule: a circle is acceptable for three to five parts of one whole with markedly different shares, and almost always it can be replaced by a single stacked bar, where shares are compared by length.

The "top 8 and other" option is worth remembering as a good technique — it rescues most overloaded charts. But here it loses for the same reason it wins elsewhere: it deliberately collapses the tail, and the tail is what the question is about.

Separately, on the "20% of products give 80% of revenue" heuristic. People expect it by default, and when the data don't bear it out there's a strong temptation to bend the wording. Here the top 20% give 36.3%, and that's a meaningful result: the portfolio is spread more evenly than is usually assumed, the risk from delisting a single SKU is lower, but there will be no easy wins off a handful of hits either. Reading your own numbers matters more than checking them against someone else's rule.

tasks.title: Three revenues at one meeting
tasks.brief: At the annual committee, three departments state 2025 revenue, and all three numbers differ. Each cites its own extract and is certain the others got it wrong. The meeting turns into an argument about numbers instead of a discussion of the plan.
tasks.goal: Determine what is actually broken here, and at what level it gets fixed.
tasks.scenario:
What the three departments said:

  sales           51 533 887 ¥
    outlet revenue at retail
    (sell-out)
  commercial      42 713 947 ¥
    shipments to distributors
    before discounts
  finance         39 104 808 ¥
    shipments after discounts
    (discounts 3 609 138 ¥, i.e. 8.4%)

All three extracts were made correctly
and are reproducible.
tasks.predictQuestion: What's broken here?

options.label: Nothing in the calculations: three departments are answering three different questions. What's broken is that the company has no settled definition of "revenue" with an owner and a place where it's written down
options.why: Each number is right in its own frame: retail sold 51.5M, we shipped 42.7M, we'll collect 39.1M. Arguing about which is "the right one" is pointless — the right one is whichever the definition names, and there is no definition.

options.label: Finance is right and the others are wrong: a company's revenue is the money it received, i.e. shipments net of discounts
options.why: For the P&L, yes. But planning a promo needs retail revenue, and assessing warehouse load needs shipments before discounts. Declaring one definition the only valid one won't settle the argument, it will move it to the next meeting.

options.label: The problem is technical: the three data sources need to be consolidated into one warehouse, and then there'll be one number
options.why: A warehouse doesn't choose between definitions — it will keep all three and add a fourth of its own. A single data mart is useful, but it's a consequence of an agreement about meaning, not a replacement for one.

options.label: It's the analyst's fault: the numbers should have been reconciled before the committee and one agreed figure brought in
options.why: Reconciling before the meeting is useful, but it treats the symptom: in a month the same thing repeats in another report. A one-off reconciliation doesn't create a rule that keeps the number the same without manual intervention.

hints: Check each number for an error: is even one of them wrong?
Ask who in the company has the right to say "revenue is calculated like this" — and where that's written down.
tasks.explain:
A discrepancy between numbers almost never means someone computed something incorrectly. Far more often everyone computed correctly — different things. Here three numbers answer three questions: how much the end shopper bought, how much we shipped, and how much of that we'll collect as cash. The gap between the first and second is the retail markup and stock sitting in the channel; between the second and third, distributor discounts, 8.4%.

Trying to pick "the right" number by vote is a dead end, because each is needed for its own task. Data governance solves it differently: the metric gets a definition, and the definition gets an owner and a place where it's recorded. The minimum set for each metric: what it's called, what exactly it counts, which tables it comes from, who is responsible for its meaning, and when it was last reviewed. A metric dictionary like that isn't bureaucracy, it's a way to avoid spending an hour of committee time on an argument in which nobody is wrong.

The practical consequence for an analyst: a metric's name has to reflect its definition. "Revenue" is a bad name because it hides a choice; "retail revenue (sell-out)" and "net shipments" are good ones, because they make the choice visible right in the column header. Half the discrepancies between reports disappear at this step, before any governance at all.

On the role of the warehouse. A single source helps once the agreement exists: it turns the agreement into code that computes identically for everyone. Without the agreement it adds one more version of the number — its own.

And on the signal that it's time to introduce definitions: if a meeting spends more than five minutes on whose number is right, the problem is no longer in the data, it's the absence of a rule. A good outcome for such a meeting isn't a chosen number, it's an assigned metric owner and a date by which the definition will be written down.

tasks.title: The reference table rewrote last year
tasks.brief: In June the outlet #1042 moved from the «Prima» chain to «Ichiba». The customer reference table was dutifully updated — the value in the chain-name column was replaced. In July a manager opens the annual report by chain for last year and can't understand why the numbers differ from the ones seen in January.
tasks.goal: Understand what happened to history, and how a reference table that doesn't do this is built.
tasks.scenario:
What changed in the report
for last year:

  in January it was
    «Prima»          8 400 000 ¥
    «Ichiba»     12 100 000 ¥
  in July it became
    «Prima»          7 900 000 ¥
    «Ichiba»     12 600 000 ¥

Last year's sales did not change.
One attribute in the customer reference
table changed — and the outlet's sales
for the whole of last year moved to the
new chain retroactively.
tasks.predictQuestion: What's the defect here?

options.label: The reference table stores only the current state, so history is reassembled to match it. An attribute that changes over time needs validity dates, so that the past is computed with what was true then
options.why: The report joins sales to the current value of the attribute and assigns the outlet's entire history to today's chain. The cure is versioning: the reference row gains start and end dates, and the join is made on the sale date.

options.label: There's no defect: a reference table should be current, and reports should reflect today's state of affairs
options.why: Currency is needed for planning the future, not for a report about the past. If history silently changes, periods can't be compared at all: any difference might turn out to be an edit to the reference table rather than a change in the business.

options.label: All past reports should be recomputed and re-sent so everyone has the same numbers
options.why: That makes the problem systematic rather than solving it: every time an outlet switches, the past gets rewritten again. And reports that decisions were already made on can't be changed retroactively — people cite them.

options.label: It's enough to save finished reports as files: then history stays fixed
options.why: A file freezes one picture but doesn't let you compute anything new under the old rules. Six months on, any new breakdown forces a choice between "as it was" and "as in the file," with nothing to reconcile them against.

hints: Sales didn't change — so what changed is the thing they're joined to. What exactly?
Ask which question the report is asking: "how much did this chain sell back then" or "how much do the outlets that are in this chain today sell."
tasks.explain:
This is the classic slowly-changing-dimension trap. The facts are immutable — last year's sales are what they always were. What changes is the reference table they're joined to, and with it all the history computed through that table.

It's important to see that both answers are legitimately needed. "How much did the «Prima» chain sell last year" is a question about history, and the outlet should count under «Prima», because that's where it was then. "How much do the outlets that belong to «Ichiba» today sell" is a question about today's portfolio, and here it's right to assign the whole history to the new chain: that's how you assess what was acquired. The defect isn't that the second option was chosen, it's that nobody made a choice — the report silently answered the second question when the first was asked.

The technical fix: the reference row gains validity dates and a current-version flag, and the old version isn't overwritten but closed off. The join between fact and dimension goes not by key alone but by date too: a March sale looks up the version of the outlet that was in force in March. That's what's called a historical dimension, and it costs more — more versions, a more complex join — so historization is switched on where an attribute really does change and does affect reports: chain, channel, region, assigned rep, product category.

A separate takeaway for an analyst who isn't building the warehouse: if history has changed on its own, look first for an edit to a reference table, not for an error in the query. The signature is distinctive — the company total still reconciles while the breakdowns have drifted apart.

And a practical habit, cheap and always useful: state in the report the date the reference data were taken as of. A line reading "chain structure as of 01.07.2026" removes half the questions and explains at once why the January version differs.

tasks.title: A request to send over an extract
tasks.brief: A consultant hired to optimize logistics writes in the work chat asking for an extract on the reps — full names, territory, outlet revenue, plan fulfillment — "to look at the data and get a picture." There is a contract with them, and the task was set by a manager.
tasks.goal: Choose what to do with a request like this.
tasks.scenario:
What's being asked for:

  rep's full name, team, territory,
  revenue of the outlets served over
  two years, monthly plan fulfillment

What's known:

  there is a contract with the consultant,
  the task is logistics optimization,
  the purpose of the extract isn't stated
  in the request, the chat is a shared one
  with about twenty people in it
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do?

options.label: Clarify which question they're solving, hand over the minimum that serves it (by territory without names, say), and send it not through the shared chat but after clearing it with the data owner
options.why: Three actions close three different risks: clarifying the purpose cuts out unnecessary fields, de-identifying removes personal data where the task doesn't need it, and the sign-off and the transfer channel record who authorized it and where it went.

options.label: Send it: there's a contract, a manager set the task, the data are internal and aren't a trade secret
options.why: A contract answers "may I work with this person," not "do they need these fields." Names alongside plan fulfillment amount to an assessment of people, and logistics can be optimized on territories and volumes.

options.label: Refuse: extracts containing personal data are never shared externally under any circumstances
options.why: A flat refusal looks safe but halts work the company paid for. Governance is about handing over exactly what's needed and leaving a trail, not about handing over nothing.

options.label: Send it to the shared chat marked "confidential, do not forward"
options.why: A marking doesn't restrict access, it only records an intention. A file in a chat of twenty people has already spread: it will be downloaded, forwarded, and found by search a year from now, long after the consultant is gone.

hints: Split the question into three: which fields this task needs, who authorizes releasing them, and by what route they'll travel.
Ask whether the logistics task can be solved without knowing anyone's surname.
tasks.explain:
The answer to a request like this consists of three independent decisions, and they must not be conflated. First, the composition of the data: which fields are genuinely needed for the stated task. Second, the basis: who in the company owns these data and authorizes the transfer. Third, the channel: how exactly they'll travel and whether a trail remains.

On composition, the principle is minimization: hand over what the task can't be solved without, and nothing beyond it. Logistics optimization works with territories, outlets, volumes and distances — the reps' surnames aren't needed for it. Drop the names, replace them with a territory code, and the task is still fully solvable while the sensitivity of the extract falls by an order of magnitude. Plan fulfillment is data about the appraisal of specific people's work, and it most likely ended up in the request simply because it sat in the same table.

On the basis: a contract is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Authorization comes from the data owner, not from whoever is technically able to run the extract. For an analyst that's protection first of all for themselves: the decision to release wasn't theirs alone and it's on record.

On the channel: a shared chat isn't a data transfer channel. A file in it can't be recalled, restricted, or traced to see who downloaded it. The minimum standard is a link with access limited to a specific person and an expiry date; better still, access to a data mart instead of a file — access can be revoked, a file can't.

And on the tone of the reply. The clarifying question "which question exactly are you solving" isn't bureaucratic resistance, it's a normal professional response: it almost always shrinks the extract, and it often turns out that what was needed wasn't a list but two numbers. Refusing with no alternative and handing over without looking are two sides of one mistake: in both, the analyst didn't do the work, they dodged the decision.

tasks.title: Bad news about someone else's work
tasks.brief: You have analysed the August «Milvara» promo for the committee. Trade marketing reported a two-and-a-half-fold increase — true in units, but in money the increase is 72%, because the 30% discount also went to the volume that would have sold without the promo. You present on Thursday, and the head of trade marketing is your most frequent internal client.
tasks.goal: Choose how to deliver a result that lands on someone you have to keep working with.
tasks.scenario:
What the analysis showed
(weekly average):

  units    1 353 → 3 327
                     +146%
  revenue  104 645 → 180 157
                      +72%
  price    77.33 → 54.15
                      −30%

The setup:

  trade marketing has quoted
  the "two and a half times"
  figure all quarter
  on Thursday he presents
  the same promo to the
  committee
  you work with him weekly
  and depend on his briefs
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do with the analysis before Thursday?

options.label: Show him the numbers and the method before the committee: not to get the conclusion approved, but so he has time to check it and bring his own explanation; present the analysis unchanged
options.why: Bad news heard publicly and for the first time turns a conversation about promo mechanics into a defence of reputation, and the argument becomes about you rather than the number. A heads-up neither softens the conclusion nor grants a veto — it removes the surprise; and it often buys you what the data does not have, such as a competitor's promo running the same weeks.

options.label: Take it to the committee as is, without warning him: showing the analysis to an interested party in advance means giving him time to prepare objections
options.why: Objections on the merits are useful, not risky, and better heard before the committee than during it. The real risk is different: someone who learns of a bad result in front of everyone starts defending himself, and the discussion drifts from "should we repeat this promo" to "whose fault is it".

options.label: Soften it: show the growth in money and the price drop, but skip the comparison with how the promo was presented all quarter
options.why: Remove the comparison and you remove the conclusion itself: the whole point is that the decision to repeat is being made on a figure twice the real effect. Gentleness that costs the reader the conclusion is not tact, it is distortion.

options.label: Hand the analysis to him and let him present it: it is his promo and his reporting, so let him decide what goes to the committee
options.why: The committee asked the question, not him, and the answer goes back to whoever asked. Handing the material to an interested party and stepping aside makes him the editor of his own assessment.

hints: For each option, picture the conversation at the committee: will it be about how the promo worked, or about who got it wrong?
One option protects the relationship at the cost of the conclusion — check what is left of the analysis once the comparison is gone.
tasks.explain:
The rule is called "no surprises": the person whose work the bad news is about hears it from you, and before the audience does. This is not about politeness. Someone caught out in public has no way to respond on the merits — he does not remember the details, has not seen the method, and is forced to defend himself; the subject quietly changes to his reputation, and the decision you did all the work for does not get made.

What a heads-up is not: it is not approval of the conclusion, not a veto, and not a reason to soften the wording. The working formula is "on Thursday I present the promo analysis, here are the numbers and the method, here is the conclusion; I want you to see it before the committee and tell me if I missed something." Give enough lead time to actually check it — a warning with no time to react is worse than none, because it reads as a formality.

In return you almost always get what the data does not hold: a competitor's promo in the same weeks, a supply gap, a change in shelf layout. Sometimes it changes the conclusion, and then you found your error before the committee rather than during it. A stakeholder with context is the cheapest reviewer you will ever get.

On wording: judge the work, not the person. "The promo delivered +72% in money at a 30% price cut" is a statement about mechanics, and one can agree with it. "Trade marketing inflated the effect" is a statement about people, and one can only argue with it. The difference in text is small; the difference in how the committee ends is enormous.

And about the pressure that will likely follow. Separate the two: wording, order, emphasis are negotiable, and giving ground there is normal and useful. The conclusion, the numbers and the caveats are not. If you do end up defending the conclusion in public, the method will already have been through its most motivated reviewer, and the argument will be about the substance rather than about who failed to warn whom.

tasks.title: Three positions and fifteen minutes
tasks.brief: The «Nettora» brand committee. Your analysis is on the screen: revenue −49%, the brand stopped selling in 46 outlets out of 79. The CFO proposes winding down support for the brand, the sales director says the numbers are wrong and the outlets are still there, the head of BI says his dashboard shows 60 active outlets. The budget decision is made today.
tasks.goal: Work out what the argument actually consists of, and what can be closed in fifteen minutes.
tasks.scenario:
Three positions at the table:

  finance
    the brand is a drag,
    wind support down
  sales
    the numbers are wrong,
    the outlets are there
  BI
    the dashboard shows 60
    active outlets, not 33

What you know:

  46 outlets had not a single
  sale of the brand all
  quarter — that is a fact
  in the BI dashboard an outlet
  stays active for a year
  after its last shipment
tasks.predictQuestion: Where do you start when you have fifteen minutes?

options.label: Split the argument into three: BI is a definition mismatch, sales is a checkable fact, finance is a decision that does not follow from the data. Close the first two on the spot, and for the third put a price on each option
options.why: The three remarks sound like one argument about numbers, but only two of them are about numbers. The definition of an active outlet and the list of 46 addresses close right there and take half the heat out of the room; "wind the brand down" is a choice of priorities, and your contribution to it is not winning but pricing each option.

options.label: Back the CFO: his conclusion matches your analysis, and he is the one making the decision anyway
options.why: Your analysis explains the cause of the decline; it does not say the brand should be wound down. The same numbers support going back into the 46 outlets just as well. By joining a side you lose the only thing that distinguishes you from everyone else at the table — having no stake in the outcome.

options.label: Suggest pausing the discussion and coming back in a week, once the three sources have been reconciled
options.why: The gap with BI closes in one sentence about definitions, and the list of 46 outlets is already in your hands: a week here buys delay, not accuracy. The budget decision will be made today regardless — only now without you.

options.label: Show that your figure is right: it is computed from sales and verified, while the BI dashboard counts shipments
options.why: Being right about method answers none of the three remarks: sales is not arguing about method, BI measures a different metric rather than a worse one, and finance is not talking about a number at all. An argument won on method leaves the decision unmade.

hints: For each remark ask: is this a claim about a fact, about a definition, or about what to do?
One of the three positions cannot be checked against data at all — which does not make it wrong.
tasks.explain:
An argument around a table is almost never homogeneous, and the first move is to sort it by type of disagreement. There are three, and each is treated differently.

Disagreement about a fact: "the outlets are still there." It is closed by a source, and not by your authority but by a checkable statement: not "my numbers are correct" but "here are 46 outlets with zero sales of the brand this quarter — name any one and we will look together." A checkable statement turns the argument into shared work; a claim about your own correctness turns it into a standoff. Often this same step teaches you something important — that three of those outlets changed owners rather than dropped the brand, for instance.

Disagreement about a definition: BI shows 60 active outlets because activity there is counted over a rolling year, while yours is sales for the quarter. Nobody is wrong here: these are two correct metrics, and confusing them is not a person's mistake but the absence of a place where the definition is written down (see dom-058: that is fixed at the level of a metric owner, not at a meeting). The right line in the room sounds boring and works: "these are different metrics; for a shelf question we need the quarterly one, and here is why."

Disagreement about a decision: "wind down support for the brand." Data does not close this at all — it is a choice of priorities, and it legitimately belongs to someone else. Your contribution is the price of the options: how much revenue sits behind the 46 outlets, what returning to the five largest gives, what another quarter of support costs. An analyst who brings a personal opinion about the priority instead of the price of the options loses both.

The interests around the table are worth remembering and not worth naming out loud. Sales has a target and a bonus on this brand, finance has a budget; that is normal, and it explains the heat. The line "you are just defending your bonus" instantly turns a working argument into a personal one and makes you a party to it. Work on the subject, not the motive.

And here is how to notice you have drifted into being a party: you start caring which position "wins". Your job is to narrow the argument down to what is checkable and hand the decision to whoever owns it, together with the cost of being wrong in either direction.

tasks.title: A metric someone else's report rests on
tasks.brief: You have been with the company three months. The weekly commercial report carries a metric called "average revenue per outlet": the team reports growth on it, and part of the quarterly bonus is tied to it. For «Nettora» it shows +22% — while the brand's revenue halved: the outlets that dropped out were smaller than the ones that stayed, and their departure lifts the average by itself.
tasks.goal: Choose how to challenge a metric that is long established and not yours.
tasks.scenario:
Metric: average revenue per
outlet. For «Nettora», +22%.

What is behind it:

  outlets that dropped out
  averaged 24 738 ¥
  those that stayed — 29 810 ¥
  like-for-like outlets grew
  by 9.7%
  the rest is the mix effect

The setup:

  the metric has been in the
  report for three years
  a bonus is tied to it
  its owner heads commercial
  analytics
  you have been here three
  months
tasks.predictQuestion: How do you challenge this metric?

options.label: Go to the metric's owner one to one with the specific case where it gives a false signal, and propose not removal but a second metric alongside it: like-for-like growth
options.why: The argument is not with the metric in general but with the decision it steers wrong: +22% while revenue halves is a case the owner will see for himself. Adding rather than replacing keeps three years of history comparable and does not require him to admit that the report has been misleading all this time.

options.label: Write it up for the general mailing list with this very example: everyone reads the metric, and staying quiet about a false signal is dishonest
options.why: You are right on the substance, but a public dissection of someone else's metric reads as an accusation, and the discussion will be about you rather than about averages. The owner is left with no way to agree without losing face — and the likeliest outcome is that the metric stays and you stop being invited.

options.label: Nothing: the metric is not yours, you have been here three months, and one figure will not outweigh three years of reporting and a bonus
options.why: Tenure is an argument neither way: the signal is either false or it is not. By staying quiet you agree to be accountable for conclusions drawn from a metric you consider wrong — and each quarter makes it harder to challenge.

options.label: Use like-for-like outlets in your own reports and show your own figure: practice will convince people better than an argument
options.why: That is how a company ends up with two numbers for the same thing and no explanation of the difference, and the first "why is yours different" turns a conversation about the signal into a fight about who counts correctly. Metrics are changed by agreement and with a change date, not unilaterally.

hints: Ask which decision is made on this metric and where exactly that decision goes wrong: what you challenge is the decision, not the number.
One option is right on the substance but chosen so that nobody can agree with it without losing face.
tasks.explain:
A metric is not challenged by the claim "it is wrong" — such a claim gets defended, and what gets defended is not the metric but the person. A metric is challenged by a case: here is a specific situation where its signal is the opposite of reality. Average revenue per outlet rising 22% while brand revenue halves is the ideal case — it does not ask anyone to take your word for it, and it can be checked in a minute.

Why "add" beats "remove". Removal touches three years of history (the series stops being comparable — the same problem as in dom-009), a bonus that has already been paid, and the author's reputation. A second metric alongside touches none of that: the old series lives on, the new one shows what the old one cannot distinguish, and the decision everyone actually cares about becomes correct. Resistance drops several-fold for the same result.

Why one to one, and before anything public: the person has to be able to agree cheaply. Agreeing in public that your metric has given a false signal for three years is expensive — expensive enough that finding an objection becomes the cheaper option. You are not "sparing feelings", you are removing the reason a correct decision would not be taken.

About "I have only been here three months". It has no bearing on whether the signal is false, and a lot of bearing on form. Three months is a good reason to ask rather than assert: "am I right that when weaker outlets drop out, the average rises on its own, even if no single outlet grew?" A question gets answered, and usually answered correctly — meaning the other person arrives at your conclusion himself. An accusation gets rebutted.

If you cannot reach agreement, there are two wrong paths and one workable one. The wrong ones are to fight in public and to quietly count your own way (that is how a company ends up with two truths). The workable one is to keep the caveat next to the figure in your own materials and take the question to where the decision that relies on the metric is made: not "to the owner's boss" but to the owner of that decision. That also surfaces the real question — whether the metric has an owner at all and whether its definition is written down anywhere (dom-058). If not, the actual problem is not the average.

tasks.title: A question the data cannot answer
tasks.brief: The sales director asks for one figure for the board: how much revenue «Nettora» lost because the brand is off the shelf in 46 outlets. Data about sales that never happened does not exist in any system.
tasks.goal: Answer without inventing a number and without leaving the requester with nothing.
tasks.scenario:
What is being asked:

  revenue lost to being off
  the shelf — one figure
  for the board

What you have:

  46 outlets with no sales
  their 2024 revenue
  the trend of like-for-like
  outlets that stayed (+9.7%)

What exists nowhere:

  what those outlets would
  have bought had the product
  been on the shelf
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you tell the sales director?

options.label: Give an estimate with the assumption named: the past revenue of those outlets, adjusted for the trend of the ones that stayed, and say plainly that this is an upper bound, not a measured loss
options.why: The board needs an order of magnitude for a decision about negotiation budget, not roubles. An estimate with its derivation written next to it delivers exactly that and stays honest: the reader can see the number came from those outlets' past rather than from measurement.

options.label: Say there is no such data: sales that never happened cannot be measured, and any number here would be invented
options.why: Formally true and practically useless. The board will name some figure anyway — just not yours, and with no assumptions attached. "There is no data" answers the question "is there data", not the question "is it worth going back into these outlets".

options.label: Compute it from the past revenue of the 46 outlets and give the number without caveats: it comes from facts, and the assumption is obvious to anyone
options.why: It is obvious to you, today. On a slide the number lives apart from how it was derived, and a month later it will be quoted as a measured loss — including by people who never saw your email. An assumption not written next to the number does not exist.

options.label: Take the brand's average revenue per outlet and multiply by 46: simple, and it needs no caveats
options.why: That is precisely the error the analysis was done to avoid: the outlets that dropped out are smaller than the ones that stayed (24 738 ¥ against 29 810 ¥), so the brand average will overstate the loss. A simple calculation is no reason to compute off the wrong base.

hints: Separate what is physically absent from the data from what can be estimated out of what you do have, with one named assumption.
For each option, check what actually lands on the board's slide and how it will be read a month later without you.
tasks.explain:
Requests like this arrive constantly, and there are three answers to them, not two: it cannot be measured — say so plainly; it can be estimated — estimate it; and the assumption goes next to the number, not into a conversation.

How the estimate is built here. The base is the past revenue of those 46 outlets specifically, not the brand average: they were smaller to begin with, and the average would overstate the answer. The adjustment is the trend of like-for-like outlets (+9.7%): had the brand stayed on the shelf, those outlets would probably have behaved like the rest. What comes out is an upper bound, and calling it an upper bound is not weakness but information: the board learns not only the size but the direction of the error. Some of that demand did not vanish — the shopper moved to a neighbouring outlet or to e-commerce, and that part is not a loss to the company.

This is why a range is usually more honest than a point. "Between a quarter and a third of the brand's quarterly revenue, likely closer to the lower end" keeps the reader away from false precision and shows what would narrow it: data on switching to nearby outlets, panel data, a measurement in the outlets you win back. A precise-looking number starts no such conversation — it just gets quoted.

"There is no data" is the most expensive form of refusal. The decision gets made anyway, on a figure someone says out loud with no assumptions attached, and the next question may not come to you.
