Work with the decision behind the request rather than with the request itself (dom-requirements): the director does not need the loss in roubles, he needs an argument about whether to spend budget getting back into those outlets — and an estimate with bounds answers that better than an exact number.

The line past which an estimate stops being one is simple: the base, the adjustment and the direction of the error must all be nameable. If none of the three can be named, it is an invented number, and then "we have nothing to measure this with" really is the honest answer. But even that should be finished properly: say what would make it measurable next time — recording the reason for a refusal in the visit log, for example. A refusal that ends in a proposal reads as work; a refusal without one reads as an excuse.

tasks.title: Asked to lead with a different number
tasks.brief: The board slide on «Nettora» is ready: revenue −49%, cause — the brand going off the shelf in 46 outlets. Your manager asks you to lead with a different figure from the same analysis, revenue per outlet at +22%: "it is true as well, and the conversation will go more calmly." Both numbers are computed correctly.
tasks.goal: Answer a request that is not a lie but changes the conclusion.
tasks.scenario:
Both figures, one analysis:

  brand revenue     −49%
  revenue per outlet +22%

Where the +22% comes from:

  46 outlets left, and they
  were smaller than the rest —
  the average rose by itself
  like-for-like outlets grew
  by 9.7%

The request:

  lead the slide with +22%,
  mention the decline if
  asked
tasks.predictQuestion: What do you do with the slide?

options.label: Keep the answer to the board's question in the headline (what is happening to the brand) and show +22% next to it as part of the explanation, with one line on where it comes from
options.why: The headline answers the question the board was convened for; +22% does not answer it but does explain the mechanics of the decline, so it belongs on the slide — just not first. The line about the mix effect also removes the temptation to read that growth as success.

options.label: Do as your manager asks: both figures are correct, and what goes in the headline is his call, not yours
options.why: Both are computed correctly, but the board will read the headline and complete the thought as "the brand is growing". Silently swapping a figure in a way that changes the conclusion is the same distortion as staying quiet about a caveat: honest numbers, false picture.

options.label: Refuse to make the slide: leading with +22% while revenue halves swaps the conclusion, and you cannot be part of that
options.why: The request is not absurd: the conversation really will turn to panic if the slide says nothing but −49%. Refusing instead of proposing turns a solvable argument about form into a conflict about your position — and the slide gets made by someone else, now without your caveats.

options.label: Put both figures in the headline side by side, −49% and +22%, and leave the link between them unexplained: let the board decide
options.why: Two opposite figures with no explanation are not honesty but handing the work back: everyone picks the one that suits their position, and the discussion becomes an argument about which is the real one. Saying how they are connected is exactly your part of the job.

hints: Ask what question the board was convened for, and whether the figure you are asked to lead with answers it.
One option formally shows everything and communicates nothing.
tasks.explain:
Distinguish pressure on form from pressure on the conclusion — they are different things, and you give ground in them differently.

Form — order, emphasis, tone, what goes first — is negotiable, and your manager is within his rights there: he knows the audience and the cost of panic in that room better than you do. The conclusion — the understanding the reader leaves with — is not negotiable. One-line test: if after the edit the reader leaves with a different picture of the situation, the edit changed the conclusion, not the form, however honestly each individual number was computed.

The +22% still belongs on the slide — as explanation, not as headline. First, without it the mechanics are unclear: the brand is not losing revenue because it sells worse where it is stocked. Second, if you leave it out, someone else will bring it in with the opposite meaning. Shown together with the mix effect, it works for the correct conclusion: growth per outlet is not an achievement but a consequence of smaller outlets leaving (dom-044).

Answer your manager with "here is how" rather than "I can't": the headline answers the board's question, +22% goes underneath with its explanation, and next to them the proposal and the price of the decision. An objection that comes with an alternative is almost always accepted; an objection without one reads as a refusal to work, and then the slide is made without you.

If he insists, remember what you do control. The numbers and the caveats do not change, but the line under the figure is yours in any case: one sentence showing that +22% is computed on a shrunken set of outlets costs little and saves the reader. When you are asked to drop that too, the argument has stopped being about form, and that is the point at which it is worth putting in writing — not to escalate, but so the decision is made visibly.

And about "so the conversation goes more calmly". The goal is not a foolish one: panic kills a sound decision just as reliably as false optimism. It is simply not achieved by choosing a figure — it is achieved by having a proposal next to the problem: what to do, what it costs, and what decision is needed from the board.

tasks.title: An error in a report already sent
tasks.brief: A day after the quarterly analysis went out you find an error: the "revenue by channel" table lost a filter, and e-commerce never made it in. The table implied the brand rests on the chains; in fact 80% of «Nettora» revenue comes from four e-commerce outlets, and the chains give 17%. The main conclusion does not change, but negotiations were opened with the chains yesterday on the strength of it.
tasks.goal: Choose how to correct an error people are already acting on.
tasks.scenario:
What went out in the report:

  chains             86%
  traditional trade  14%
  e-commerce   no row at all

What is actually true:

  e-commerce   869k   80%
  chains       180k   17%
  traditional   30k    3%

Forty people read the report,
negotiations with the chains
started yesterday. The finding
about 46 outlets still holds.
tasks.predictQuestion: How do you correct it?

options.label: Write immediately to the people whose decision rests on that table: with the corrected figures and an explicit line, "the main conclusion is unchanged, the priority changes"; a short correction follows to the other forty
options.why: Negotiations are happening today, so speed matters more than completeness of explanation. Splitting it into "what did not change / what did" lets the reader work out in ten seconds whether the correction touches their actions, without rereading the whole report.

options.label: Quietly replace the table in the file and the dashboard: the figures become correct, and making noise over one table only draws attention to your mistake
options.why: People are acting on the version they saw, and the corrected file will not reach them; the discrepancy will surface in a meeting where someone is holding a printout. A silent fix turns one error into two — a wrong table, and no way to tell which version to trust.

options.label: Write to all forty with a detailed apology and an explanation of how the error got into the report
options.why: The people running negotiations need ten seconds to decide whether to change the plan; a detailed act of contrition does not give them that and pushes the point to the end of the message. The root cause matters, but separately, later, and as what now stands between you and the next error of this kind.

options.label: Fix it in next week's regular report: the table will be right there, and a separate message would only confuse people
options.why: A week is a week of negotiating with the channel that gives 17% of the brand's revenue instead of the one that gives 80%. The cost of silence is not measured in awkwardness but in the work of people acting on your figure.

hints: Ask whose action tomorrow changes because of this correction — that is where the recipient list starts.
One option makes the correction invisible to exactly the people already acting on the old version.
tasks.explain:
Correcting an error that has already reached people has an order to it, and it does not start with apologies.

First: who is acting on this figure. Not "all forty recipients" but those whose action tomorrow changes — the team that opened talks with the chains. They are written to first and immediately, because every hour of work on the wrong priority is paid for. Second: what exactly is wrong, in which direction and by how much — not "there was an error in the table" but "e-commerce was missing from the breakdown; it accounts for 80% of the brand's revenue, the chains for 17%". Third, and this is what gets skipped most often: what has not changed. The main finding about the 46 lost outlets stands. Without that line, a reader who does not know the boundaries of the error quite reasonably stops trusting the whole document, flawless parts included. A stated boundary works the same way as a stated weakness in the data in dom-054: it shows you know where your knowledge ends.

Everyone else gets the short correction next, one paragraph. And only then, in a separate message and without rushing, the cause and what has changed in the process so it does not recur.

The silent fix looks like the cheapest way out and is the most expensive. People made a decision on the version they saw; two files with the same name will be left in the correspondence, and a month later nobody will be able to prove which table was on the table when the decision was made. The rule is simple: the corrected version carries a date and a "what changed" line, and the old one is not deleted but marked superseded (dom-059).

On apologies: one sentence is enough, then get to the substance. A long act of contrition moves attention from the reader's decision to your feelings and damages trust more than the error itself: the recipient starts to feel something extraordinary happened, when what happened was a lost filter.

And the root cause, properly. It is not "carelessness" — nothing protects against carelessness. It is the absence of the check that catches this class of error: a breakdown must add up to the report's total. Chains plus traditional trade came to 210 thousand against brand revenue of 1 079 thousand — a discrepancy visible in a second, if anyone does that reconciliation at all. That is the pre-send check (dom-sanity-check): every breakdown of one quantity gives the same total, and when it does not, the thing to look at is not the breakdown but the filter.
